title: The First Declension — Feminine in α
subtitle: ἡ θάλασσα, ἡ μοῖρα, ἡ ἡμέρα — long and short alpha.
objectives: Decline first-declension feminine nouns ending in -α in all five cases and both numbers.
Distinguish long α (after ε, ι, ρ) from short α (after other consonants).
Recognize the genitive singular ending -ας or -ης depending on vowel length.
Parse first-declension feminine nouns in -α on sight.

sections.heading: Alpha instead of eta
sections.body:
Some first-declension feminines end in -α instead of -η. The pattern is almost identical to the -η nouns, but the singular uses α where the -η nouns used η.

There are two sub-types: long α and short α. Long α appears after ε, ι, or ρ. Short α appears after other consonants. The difference matters only in the genitive and dative singular.

Long α nouns: genitive singular -ας (not -ης), dative singular -ᾳ (not -ῃ).
Short α nouns: genitive singular -ης (like the -η nouns), dative singular -ῃ.

The plural is identical for all first-declension feminines.

sections.heading: The paradigm: ἡ θάλασσα (sea) — long α
sections.body:
singular        plural
  nominative  θάλασσα         θάλασσαι
  genitive    θαλάσσης        θαλασσῶν
  dative      θαλάσσῃ         θαλάσσαις
  accusative  θάλασσαν        θαλάσσας
  vocative    θάλασσα         θάλασσαι

Wait — this is short α (the sigma is not ε, ι, or ρ). Let me correct:

ἡ μοῖρα (fate, portion) — long α after ρ:
              singular        plural
  nominative  μοῖρα           μοῖραι
  genitive    μοίρας          μοιρῶν
  dative      μοίρᾳ           μοίραις
  accusative  μοῖραν          μοίρας
  vocative    μοῖρα           μοῖραι

ἡ ἡμέρα (day) — long α after ρ:
              singular        plural
  nominative  ἡμέρα           ἡμέραι
  genitive    ἡμέρας          ἡμερῶν
  dative      ἡμέρᾳ           ἡμέραις
  accusative  ἡμέραν          ἡμέρας
  vocative    ἡμέρα           ἡμέραι

The genitive and dative singular have α, not η, because α is long after ρ.

sections.heading: Short α: ἡ θάλασσα
sections.body:
singular        plural
  nominative  θάλασσα         θάλασσαι
  genitive    θαλάσσης        θαλασσῶν
  dative      θαλάσσῃ         θαλάσσαις
  accusative  θάλασσαν        θαλάσσας
  vocative    θάλασσα         θάλασσαι

The genitive and dative singular use η (θαλάσσης, θαλάσσῃ) because the α is short.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Cover the answers. Parse each form or answer each question.

items.prompt: When does α remain α in the genitive and dative singular?
items.answer: When it is long — after ε, ι, or ρ.

items.prompt: When does α change to η in the genitive and dative singular?
items.answer: When it is short — after consonants other than ρ.

items.prompt: Are the plural endings the same for all first-declension feminines?

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 2.6 introduces the first-declension masculines: ὁ ποιητής, ὁ νεανίας. These are masculine nouns that follow the first declension instead of the second. They take the masculine article but use first-declension endings.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can distinguish long α from short α and can decline both types correctly.
